sections.title: One door, one ledger, many loops
paras: Strip away the deployment diagrams and Kubernetes has one shape: a hub with spokes. At the hub sits the API server, a stateless HTTP server that exposes every object in the cluster — Pods (the unit of one or more running containers), Nodes (the machines they run on), and everything else — as REST resources you read and write. Behind it sits etcd, a replicated key-value store that holds the cluster's entire state. Every other component in the system is a client of that one API, and nothing more.

Walk the roster and the pattern holds. The scheduler, which picks a node for each new Pod; the controller manager, which hosts the loops that push actual state toward desired state; the kubelet, the agent on every node that starts and stops containers; kubectl, the CLI; your CI pipeline — each is an authenticated API client, no different in kind from a shell script calling curl. None of them talk to each other. When the scheduler places a Pod it does not contact a kubelet: it writes the assignment through the API server, and the kubelet — watching the API for Pods bound to its node — sees the new record and acts on it.

By design, etcd accepts connections from exactly one client: the API server. No controller, no node, no dashboard has a route to the store. That single door is where authentication, authorization, and audit logging happen — once, identically, whether the caller is a kubelet or an intern's laptop. The failure mode this kills is the one most systems accrete over years: a dozen components holding their own database credentials, each enforcing its own idea of validation, none producing a coherent audit trail.

The control-plane spokes hold no durable state of their own. A controller keeps an in-memory cache of the objects it cares about, built by listing them from the API and then watching for changes; on restart it discards everything and rebuilds from scratch. There is no local database to corrupt, no snapshot to restore, no state-transfer handshake between replicas. If losing a control-plane component's disk loses information, the design is broken.

That statelessness is what makes the control plane crash-only. Kill the scheduler with kill -9 and new Pods queue up unassigned until it returns, rebuilds its view, and drains the backlog; kill the controller manager and self-healing pauses, then converges. Kubernetes does not lean on graceful shutdown, because a shutdown protocol only protects you when processes exit politely, and the outage you care about is the one where they don't. Here the crash path and the clean-exit path are the same path, so the recovery code runs on every restart instead of rotting until the incident that needed it.

Hold the control plane — the components that decide: API server, etcd, scheduler, controllers — apart from the data plane, the nodes where your containers execute. Take the entire control plane down and running containers keep running: kubelets keep supervising them locally, and traffic keeps flowing along routes already programmed into each node. What stops is change — no new rollouts, no rescheduling off a dead node, no scaling. You lose the ability to change things, not the things themselves. A control-plane outage degrades agility, not service.

The dividends are operational. Debugging means querying one API: desired state and reported actual state sit side by side, inspectable with kubectl get, because there is nowhere else for shared state to live. Components are independently replaceable — swap the stock scheduler for your own, run custom controllers beside the built-in ones, upgrade pieces one at a time — because the API is the only contract any of them share. One door, one ledger, many loops: the sections that follow are the mechanics that make each third of that slogan hold.
sections.pattern: Put one gateway in front of one authoritative store, and make every other component a stateless, crash-restartable client that rebuilds its world from that store on startup. Components then coordinate by writing records that others observe — coordination becomes data, which makes it auditable, replayable, and inspectable in ways an RPC chain never is.

misconception.wrong: Newcomers picture an RPC pipeline: kubectl calls the API server, which calls the scheduler, which calls the kubelet, each command flowing forward until the container starts.
misconception.right: No component calls another. Each writes records into the shared store through the API server and independently watches for records that concern it — a Pod starts because several watchers each reacted to state, not because anyone issued a command.

sections.title: etcd: one history, in order
paras: Everything the control plane knows — every Pod (the unit of one or more containers that run together), every piece of configuration, every record of what should exist — lives as a value in etcd, a replicated key-value store. Keep that store on one machine and the machine is a single point of failure for the entire cluster. Replicate it naively — two copies, both accepting writes — and a network partition produces split-brain: each half keeps accepting writes, and you end up with two divergent histories that no merge can honestly reconcile. The problem consensus solves is not durability; it is agreement — after any failure, exactly one history survives.

etcd stays consistent by running Raft, a consensus protocol built around one replicated, append-only log. At any moment one member is the leader, and all writes flow through it. The leader appends each write to its log, streams the entry to its followers, and declares it committed only once a majority — a quorum — has persisted it. If the leader dies, followers stop hearing its heartbeats, wait out an election timeout of roughly a second, and elect a replacement under a new term, a monotonically increasing epoch number. A revived old leader can no longer commit anything: any majority it needs overlaps the majority that elected its successor, those members reject its stale term, and the moment it sees the higher term it steps down.

The quorum arithmetic decides how many members to run. A majority of 3 is 2, so a 3-member cluster survives one loss; a majority of 5 is 3, so it survives two. A majority of 4 is also 3 — a 4-member cluster still survives only one loss, while adding replication traffic and one more machine that can fail. Even sizes buy nothing, which is why production control planes run 3 or 5 members, never 4. And when quorum is lost entirely, etcd refuses writes rather than guess: unavailable beats divergent.

etcd is also an MVCC store — multi-version concurrency control. It never overwrites a value in place; every write, to any key, increments a single global counter called the revision and records a new version stamped with it. That counter is a logical clock for the whole store: revision 4,000,001 happened after 4,000,000, with no wall clocks and no clock-skew arguments. Kubernetes surfaces it as the resourceVersion field carried by every object — a position in the cluster's one totally ordered history of changes — though the API contract asks clients to treat it as opaque: something you hand back, never a number you parse or compare.

Because every change carries a revision, etcd can honor a request no ordinary database offers: watch these keys starting from revision N, send me every change since then in order, and keep streaming. A client that disconnects does not lose its place — it reconnects and resumes from the last revision it saw, missing nothing. This watch-from-a-revision stream is the primitive the entire control plane is built on; every cache, controller, and scheduler in the sections ahead is a subscriber to it.

Keeping every version of every key forever would grow the database without bound, so etcd compacts: on a schedule, it discards versions older than some revision. That creates one sharp edge. A watcher that fell far behind — a component that was down for an hour, say — may ask to resume from a revision that no longer exists. etcd answers that the revision has been compacted, and Kubernetes surfaces this as HTTP 410 Gone. Such a watcher cannot be replayed forward; it must re-read current state and start watching from there — resynchronization is a designed-for event, not an emergency.

One more boundary makes all of this scale: nothing in the cluster talks to etcd except the API server — not the kubelet on each node, not controllers, not kubectl. Part of the reason is policy enforcement, which section 03 covers. The other part is load: a large cluster runs tens of thousands of watchers, and a store that pays a round of consensus per write cannot also serve every one of them. So the API server keeps a watch cache — an in-memory, per-resource copy of recent state, fed by its own single watch against etcd — and serves nearly all watches and much of the read traffic from it. Consensus is paid once per write and amortized across every reader.
sections.pattern: Pay for consensus exactly once, at a single replicated log that stamps every change with a global monotonic version, and make everything else a disposable subscriber that resumes from a version — or re-reads and re-subscribes when it falls too far behind. The product is order, not storage: a change feed with exact positions turns caching, replication, and crash recovery into the same operation.

misconception.wrong: etcd is where Kubernetes keeps its data — a database that cluster components query and update the way an application talks to Postgres.
misconception.right: Only the API server ever touches etcd, and most reads never reach it at all. What etcd actually provides is ordering: one agreed-upon history of changes with positions you can subscribe from — the key-value storage is almost incidental.

beats: A write arrives at the leader of a 3-node etcd cluster and is appended to its log.
The entry streams to both followers; the moment a second node persists it, it flashes as committed.

sections.title: A pipeline, not a brain
paras: Strip away the mythology and the Kubernetes API server (kube-apiserver) is a REST server in front of a key-value store. It does not schedule pods onto nodes, does not restart failed containers, does not compare desired state to actual state. The API server is a validating, versioning storage gateway — every piece of cluster intelligence lives in its clients. The scheduler, the controllers, the kubelet on each node: all of them are ordinary API clients with no private channel. Keeping the gateway generic means it can serve a type it has never heard of, and can scale by adding replicas rather than by getting smarter.

Follow one write through it — kubectl apply (the CLI submitting a manifest) creating a Deployment, the object that declares a replicated application. First, authentication answers who are you: client TLS certificates, bearer tokens for in-cluster service accounts, or OIDC (OpenID Connect) tokens from an external identity provider. Authentication produces an identity — a username plus groups — and approves no action. Separating identity from permission means you can swap identity providers without touching a single access rule.

Next, authorization answers may you. RBAC (role-based access control) grants an identity verbs — get, list, create, patch, delete — on resources, optionally scoped to a namespace. Note what RBAC cannot express: it has no opinion about the contents of the object, only about who touches which resource with which verb. Content rules come later in the pipeline, and the division is deliberate — a cheap identity-level check rejects illegitimate traffic before the server spends effort on the payload.

Now the object goes through admission. Schema defaults were stamped in when the request was decoded; mutating admission goes further — built-in plugins apply cluster-level defaults, and mutating webhooks, external HTTP services you register, may rewrite the object, which is how sidecar injection works. Then the mutated object is validated against its schema, and last come validating admission webhooks, which may veto but are forbidden to change a byte. The ordering is the security property: validation and policy always see the final object, so no mutation can slip in after a check has passed. Reverse it and a mutating webhook could alter an object after your policy engine approved it.

Only now is the object written, and here versioning earns its keep. A resource is served at several API versions at once — a group/version like apps/v1 is a wire contract, not a storage format. Internally the server converts every request through a hub version — each of n served versions needs one converter to the hub, not n² pairwise converters — and persists at exactly one storage version. Serialize, write to etcd (the consistent store from the previous section), return. Clients on old and new versions read the same underlying object, which is what lets a cluster upgrade its API without a flag-day migration.

One structural detail does heavy lifting: /status is a subresource, a separate endpoint on the same object. A write to the main resource cannot touch status; a write to /status cannot touch spec. Users write spec — intent — while controllers write status — observation — and RBAC can grant each side only its half. Without the split, a user could forge "this pod is healthy," and no rule could let a controller report observations without also letting it rewrite intent.

Because the pipeline contains no per-type logic, a new type is configuration, not code. Post a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) — a schema plus a group/version/kind name — and the API server starts serving the new resource: storage in etcd, RBAC on its verbs, watch streams, kubectl get, multiple served versions (you supply a conversion webhook when schemas differ). A CRD buys your custom type the entire machine for the price of a schema. That is the mechanism behind the operator ecosystem: write a controller for your database or message queue, and it plugs into the same pipeline the built-in types use.

Finally, notice what the pipeline never needed: memory. Every durable fact lives in etcd, so the API server holds no state a crash could lose. Run three of them behind a load balancer, all active, no leader election — any replica can serve any request, and killing one loses nothing but its open connections. Components that make decisions must elect a leader to avoid dueling actors; a gateway that decides nothing has nothing to duel over. When you hear that Kubernetes control planes scale horizontally, this is the component doing it.
sections.pattern: Keep the gateway dumb: put one generic, stateless authenticate-validate-version-store pipeline in front of your database and push all domain intelligence into clients of its public API. The gateway then scales by replication with no election, and new object types cost a schema instead of a code change.

misconception.wrong: The API server is the brain of the cluster — it decides where pods run, notices failures, and drives the system toward the desired state.
misconception.right: It decides nothing about the cluster. It authenticates, authorizes, mutates, validates, versions, and stores; scheduling and reconciling are done by separate components that are ordinary clients of the same API you use.

sections.title: No locks, only retries
paras: Start with the design Kubernetes rejected: when dozens of controllers write to the same objects, the reflex is to serialize them — take a lock, mutate, release. But a distributed lock is a liability with a failure mode attached. The holder crashes mid-update and the lock stays held forever, so you add a TTL; now a holder stalled in a long GC pause has its lock expire while it still believes it owns it, so you add fencing tokens, and every participant must thread tokens through every operation. Each patch to pessimistic locking adds a new machine that can itself fail. Kubernetes opts out of the entire ladder: no write to an object ever waits on a lock.

The alternative rides on a field you have already met. Every object carries metadata.resourceVersion: an opaque string stamped by the storage layer — underneath, the etcd MVCC revision from section 02 — naming the write that produced the copy you hold. When you PUT an update, you send the object back carrying the resourceVersion you read. If any other writer touched the object since your read, the versions differ and the API server rejects your write with 409 Conflict. The server never blocks a writer; it refuses stale ones.

Every controller is built around the same loop: GET the object, apply your change in memory, PUT it back, and on 409 re-GET the fresh copy and reapply the change. The client library ships this as a helper (retry.RetryOnConflict in client-go) because it is not an error path — it is the ordinary cost of concurrency. A controller that loses the race loses one round trip, and its intent lands on the next attempt. A busy cluster's API server metrics show a steady background rate of 409s: contention being resolved, not something breaking.

This is compare-and-swap, lifted from a CPU instruction to an HTTP API. Each write says "replace the object only if it is still at the version I read" — the contract of an atomic CAS on a shared word, and it inherits the same property: coordination is lock-free. Dozens of writers make progress concurrently, none ever waits on another, and a writer that crashes mid-loop leaves nothing behind — no lock to expire, no session to clean up. A dead writer costs the system nothing, which is the guarantee pessimistic locking can never give you. That is what makes the crash-only design from section 01 possible: any component may die at any instant without ceremony.

One version number is not enough, because resourceVersion is too sensitive. It changes on every write — a status update, a new annotation, another controller's touch — so it cannot answer the question you actually have after kubectl apply: has the controller acted on my change yet? For that, objects carry metadata.generation, which the API server increments only when the spec — the desired state — changes. Controllers write back status.observedGeneration, the generation they most recently processed. If status.observedGeneration lags metadata.generation, every status field describes your previous intent; a Deployment can report healthy moments after you pushed a broken image, and comparing these two numbers is how you avoid believing it.

Compare-and-swap protects whole objects, but many objects have several legitimate owners at the field level: a deploy pipeline sets the container image, the horizontal autoscaler sets replicas, a policy tool maintains labels. The version check cannot referee this, because the danger is not staleness: a pipeline re-applying its full manifest holds a fresh resourceVersion, and its write legally resets replicas to whatever the manifest says — the classic read-modify-write clobber. Server-side apply makes ownership per-field: the API server records in metadata.managedFields which manager set which field, each writer submits only the fields it cares about, and the server merges — raising a conflict only when two managers claim the same field. The unit of ownership drops from the object to the field, so co-ownership stops being a race.

Some jobs still want a single active actor — you do not want two scheduler instances binding pods against each other. Kubernetes does not reintroduce locks for this either: it builds leader election out of the same conditional-write primitive, a CAS on a Lease object, which section 10 takes apart. The idea to carry away: give every record a version, make every write conditional on the version the writer read, and push retries to the edges. You get coordination among any number of writers with no lock service to operate — and nothing to clean up when one of them dies.
sections.pattern: Version every record and make every write conditional on the version the writer read; reject stale writes with a retryable error instead of making writers wait. Any number of writers can then coordinate without a lock service, and a writer that crashes mid-operation leaves nothing to expire, fence, or clean up.

misconception.wrong: A 409 Conflict means something went wrong — two components writing to the same object at once is a race that Kubernetes must be preventing with a lock somewhere.
misconception.right: There is no lock anywhere; concurrent writers losing races is the designed steady state. Well-behaved clients wrap writes in a re-GET-and-retry loop, and a background rate of 409s on a busy cluster is contention being resolved, not malfunction.

beats: Two controllers each GET the same object; both copies show resourceVersion 41.
Controller A PUTs first — the server accepts, and the object ticks to version 42.
Controller B PUTs its stale copy at 41 — the write bounces off with a red 409 Conflict; the object is untouched.
B re-GETs the fresh object at 42, reapplies its change, PUTs again — accepted at 43.

before: When dozens of controllers write to the same objects, the reflex is to serialize them — take a lock, mutate, release. But a distributed lock is a liability with a failure mode attached. Each patch to pessimistic locking adds a new machine that can itself fail.

The unit of ownership drops from the object to the field, so co-ownership stops being a race. sections.title: Watch, do not poll
paras: Start with the arithmetic. A production cluster holds tens of thousands of objects — Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, EndpointSlices — and dozens of control loops each need to notice when any of them changes. If every loop polled the API server once a second, that is hundreds of thousands of object reads per second pressed against a store that replicates through a Raft quorum. And polling has no good frequency: poll fast and you melt etcd, poll slow and every reaction waits out the interval. Polling charges you for reads whether or not anything changed; a watch makes cost proportional to the rate of change.

Kubernetes replaces polling with a two-step contract called list+watch. A LIST request returns a consistent snapshot of every object of one type, stamped with the resourceVersion at which it was taken — the etcd revision counter from the storage section, a cluster-wide logical clock. A WATCH opened from that version streams every subsequent change as an ordered sequence of ADDED, MODIFIED, and DELETED events, with no gaps. A consistent snapshot plus an ordered, gap-free stream of deltas is a replication protocol: the client maintains a perfect local replica for the cost of one open HTTP connection. Drop either guarantee — ordering or no-gaps — and the replica silently corrupts.

Watch connections die routinely: an API server restarts, a load balancer times out an idle stream, a network path flaps. The client reconnects and asks to watch from the last resourceVersion it saw, and the server replays whatever was missed — the failure leaves no trace in the replica. The one case that cannot be replayed is a version so old that the server has already compacted that history away. It then answers 410 Gone and the client relists: full snapshot, new version, fresh stream. Relists are the expensive path, so the server periodically sends bookmark events — an otherwise-empty object carrying only the current resourceVersion — so that even a watcher on a quiet resource never falls far behind.

The client library, client-go, packages this loop so no controller author writes it by hand. A reflector runs list+watch and pushes each delta into a DeltaFIFO: a queue keyed by object, so all pending changes to one object accumulate under a single key and pop together. An informer pops from that queue, applies each delta to an indexed in-memory cache — lookups by namespace, by name, by any index you register — and then calls the event handlers you attached. Your code never touches the wire protocol; it sees a local, ordered, queryable replica of the server's state.

Informers are shared. A single process often hosts many controllers — kube-controller-manager, the binary that runs the built-in control loops, holds dozens — and a shared informer opens one watch stream per resource type per process, no matter how many controllers subscribe. They all read the same cache. The API server is consulted on writes and once per type for the stream — never per decision. Without sharing, connections would scale as controllers times types and every decision would become a remote read; with it, a controller's read costs a map lookup.

Event handlers are deliberately forbidden from doing the work. A handler extracts a key — namespace/name — and enqueues it into a workqueue; nothing else. The reason is placement: each subscriber's handlers run in order on one dispatch goroutine, so a handler that blocks on I/O stalls every later event bound for that subscriber while the undelivered backlog piles up in memory. The key is also where duplicates collapse: ten rapid updates to one object become one queued key. What pops that key and acts on it is the next section's subject.

One safety net remains. On a configurable interval — minutes or hours, not seconds — the informer resyncs: it replays every object already in its cache through your handlers as update events. This is not a relist; the server is never contacted. It exists because edge-triggered systems die by dropped edges — a handler bug, a crash between dequeue and action, a delta mishandled once. The resync re-presents the full current state on a clock, so any object whose processing was lost gets enqueued again and repaired — a missed event costs latency, never correctness.
sections.pattern: When many consumers must react to changes in shared state, do not let them poll the store. Hand each one a consistent snapshot stamped with a version, then an ordered, gap-free stream of deltas from that version: each consumer maintains a local replica and serves its own reads, so the source of truth pays one stream per consumer instead of one query per decision.

sections.title: Levels, not edges
paras: There are two ways to make a system respond to change. An edge-triggered system reacts to each change notification as it arrives — the notification is the work; a level-triggered system compares the full desired state against the full actual state and corrects the difference — a notification carries no information beyond look now. The distinction sounds academic until a process crashes in the gap between receiving an event and acting on it. An edge-triggered system that misses one edge drifts permanently; a level-triggered system converges from any starting state. The lost event never gets redelivered; the next comparison happens regardless.

Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered. A controller is a loop that drives one slice of the cluster — the actual state of some set of objects — toward the desired state declared in their spec. Watch events from the previous section still flow into every controller, but they are demoted to hints about when to look, never inputs to what to do. Miss an event and you lose freshness until the next hint or periodic resync — you never lose correctness.

You can read this commitment straight off the function signature. A reconcile function receives one argument: a key — a namespace/name string such as payments/api — not the event that woke it, not old and new object versions, not a diff. Because the function cannot know what changed, it is forced to re-observe everything. It reads desired state from the informer cache — the local, watch-maintained copy of the API server's data — observes actual state, computes the minimal action that closes the gap, and acts. Nothing else is trusted as input.

Between the event stream and the workers sits a workqueue, and its first property is collapse: a key is queued at most once, no matter how many events name it while it waits. Ten rapid updates to one object become one pending reconcile. This is only safe because the queue item carries no payload — since reconcile re-reads the entire current state, running once after the tenth event produces exactly what running ten times would. Under an update storm, work stays bounded by the number of objects, not the number of events.

The queue's second property: the same key is never handed to two workers at once, so two reconciles of one object cannot race each other into creating duplicate children or issuing conflicting writes — different keys still run in parallel. Third: a failed reconcile requeues its key with per-key exponential backoff, starting at milliseconds and capping near the scale of minutes. Why per-key: one object that persistently fails — a bad image reference, a webhook that rejects it — backs off alone, without hammering the API server or starving the healthy keys around it.

Idempotency is not a virtue here; it is a load-bearing requirement. Any reconcile may run twice — a resync, a duplicate hint, a crash after acting but before the key was marked done. It may also run against a world where the work is already finished. So creating a child that already exists must degrade to a no-op — treat a 409 AlreadyExists as success — and deleting one already gone must swallow the 404. The loop's contract is converge to desired, never perform this action exactly once.

The final discipline: a controller never trusts its own writes. After acting, it does not update its local beliefs — no I created it, so it exists flag. The write may have failed, been mutated by an admission webhook, or been reverted by another actor seconds later; the next loop observes reality again and finds out. A crash mid-reconcile loses no progress, because no progress is stored — only state is. A restarted controller relists the world, reconciles everything, and convergence resumes as if nothing happened.

This is the machinery under the loop the 3D walkthrough shows closing the gap between desired and actual. Strip away the Kubernetes nouns and one trade remains: the system refuses to depend on exactly-once event delivery — a guarantee distributed systems cannot cheaply give — and pays for that refusal with redundant reads. Reads are cheap, served from a local cache. Missed messages are catastrophic. Kubernetes buys correctness with the cheaper currency.
sections.pattern: Never let correctness depend on delivering every event: store desired state durably, make workers pure functions of a key that re-observe full state and converge, and treat notifications only as cache-invalidation hints that say "look now." You trade cheap redundant reads for immunity to lost messages, duplicate delivery, and mid-action crashes.

sections.title: Controllers compose
paras: You run an application by creating a Deployment: an object holding a pod template, a replica count, and an update strategy. Watch what happens next and you will notice something odd. The Deployment controller never creates a pod. It creates and resizes ReplicaSets — objects whose entire specification amounts to "keep N pods matching this template alive" — and touches nothing below them. The ReplicaSet controller, one layer down, counts the pods it owns that match its label selector, compares the count to spec.replicas, and creates or deletes pods to close the gap.

This ignorance is the design, not a limitation. The ReplicaSet controller has no concept of a rolling update, a revision, or a rollback; that vocabulary does not exist at its layer. The Deployment controller does not know how pods get scheduled or restarted. Each loop maintains one invariant it can state in a sentence, which means each loop can be tested by handing it a cluster state and checking what it writes.

A rolling update is arithmetic on two ReplicaSets. When you change the Deployment's pod template, the controller hashes the new template, creates a fresh ReplicaSet for it, and then, pass after pass, scales the new one up and the old one down — total pods never exceeding the desired count by more than maxSurge, available pods never dipping below it by more than maxUnavailable. There is no rollout plan persisted anywhere. The replica counts of the two ReplicaSets are the entire state of the rollout. A workflow engine that dies mid-sequence leaves you asking whether step four executed; kill this controller mid-update and its replacement reads two integers and resumes, because there are no steps — only a gap between two numbers.

Rollback falls out of the same arithmetic. A bounded number of old ReplicaSets are kept at zero replicas as revision history, so rolling back means setting the Deployment's template back to the previous one: the controller finds the existing ReplicaSet whose template matches and scales it up while scaling the current one down. Rollback runs through the identical code path as rollout — it is exactly as well-tested as the thing it undoes.

Deletion composes the same way, through data instead of calls. Every child records its parent in metadata.ownerReferences: each Pod names its ReplicaSet, each ReplicaSet names its Deployment. The garbage collector — itself one more controller, watching every resource type and maintaining a graph of who owns whom — deletes any object whose owner no longer exists. Delete a Deployment and the cascade follows without a single message between controllers: the ReplicaSets lose their owner and go, then their Pods. This closes off a classic failure mode — a parent that must enumerate and clean up its own descendants can crash halfway and leak the rest, but here the deletion intent lives in the data, where any later pass will find it.

kube-controller-manager, one of the control plane's standing processes, is a single binary hosting dozens of these loops: node lifecycle, endpoints, namespace, service account, job, cronjob, the garbage collector, and more. Sharing a process is a packaging decision, not an architectural one. The loops share informer caches — the watch machinery from earlier — but no logic and no private channels; every effect one loop has on another travels through objects in the API server.

Weigh this against the alternative: one orchestrator that understands the whole plan, from user intent down to individual containers. That component's state machine grows with every feature, its failure takes everything down, and testing it means simulating everything it touches. Small loops invert each cost. A logic bug in the loop managing Jobs (run-to-completion workloads) can mangle Jobs, but rollouts keep working, because the two loops share nothing but the process they run in. Each loop is testable in isolation, and the seams between layers are public API objects rather than internal interfaces.

Public seams are what make the system extensible. A controller you write talks to the same API server and uses the same watches and the same conflict-checked writes as the built-in ones — the control plane cannot tell your controller from its own. This is what an operator is: a custom controller, typically paired with a custom resource type (a CRD), that encodes operational knowledge — provision a database, rotate its certificates, take backups. Set ownerReferences on what it creates and the garbage collector cleans up after it; have it create Deployments and the entire rollout stack runs beneath you, unmodified.
sections.pattern: Decompose orchestration into a stack of small reconcilers, each owning exactly one parent-child relationship and communicating only through shared declarative state, never through calls to each other. Cross-cutting concerns like cleanup become one more reconciler over the same state, and because the seams are public data, third parties can add layers you never anticipated.

misconception.wrong: The Deployment controller is an end-to-end orchestrator: it creates pods, watches them come up, and executes a scripted sequence of rollout steps.
misconception.right: It only writes ReplicaSet objects — pods are two layers away — and no component holds the rollout as a plan. The rollout's only state is the replica counts of two ReplicaSets, which is why a controller crash mid-update loses nothing.

sections.title: The scheduler: filter, score, bind
paras: The scheduler sounds like it should be the most privileged component in the system: it decides which node — which worker machine — runs each pod. Yet it has no privileged interface at all. The scheduler is one more watch client, queueing every pod whose spec.nodeName is empty. It holds no lock on the cluster and no channel to the nodes; its entire authority is RBAC permission to set one field. Stop it and bind a pod by hand — POST the same request yourself — and the cluster cannot tell the difference.

For each pod it pops from its queue, the scheduler runs a two-phase pipeline over the candidate nodes. The first phase, filter, removes nodes that cannot take the pod: not enough unreserved CPU or memory (measured against the pod's declared requests, not live usage, so placement does not flap with load), a taint — a repellent marker on the node — that the pod's tolerations do not accept, an anti-affinity rule ("never on the same node as X"), or a requested host port already claimed. These are hard constraints. A node that fails one check is out; there is no partial credit.

The second phase, score, ranks the survivors. Each score plugin returns a number per node — roughly zero to one hundred — and the scheduler multiplies by the plugin's weight and sums: spread a service's pods across zones and nodes, prefer less-allocated nodes (or more-allocated, if you want bin-packing), prefer nodes that already hold the container image. Keeping filter and score separate keeps "cannot" out of the cost function. A single blended fitness score would let enough preference points outvote a hard constraint, and a pod would land somewhere it cannot run.

Then comes the step people expect to be the dramatic one, and it is a write. The scheduler POSTs a Binding to the pod's binding subresource, which sets spec.nodeName: one field flips from empty to a node's name in etcd, and the scheduler's work on that pod is finished. It launches nothing and contacts no node. The kubelet — the agent on each node — watches for pods bound to its own name, sees the new record, and does the launching (section 09). Placement is a row in the ledger like everything else.

Why record the decision instead of executing it? Because the record outlives the decider. If the scheduler crashes a millisecond after the write commits, nothing is lost: the pod is bound, the kubelet proceeds, and no handshake was left half-open. A scheduler that pushed launch commands over connections to nodes would have to answer what happens when a connection drops mid-command — Kubernetes never has to ask the question.

When filtering leaves zero nodes, the scheduler has one more move. Pods carry a priority (assigned through a PriorityClass), and the scheduler searches for a node where evicting enough lower-priority pods would make this one fit. It deletes those victims — they get their graceful shutdown — records the choice in the pod's status.nominatedNodeName, and retries on a later pass; the nomination is a hint, not a reservation, and the re-run may choose differently. Without preemption, a cluster full of batch work would lock out a critical pod forever: priority means nothing if arrival order always wins.

Now kill the scheduler and watch what does not happen. Every running pod keeps running and every service keeps serving, because the scheduler sits in the decision path for new pods, never in the data path or the launch path. New pods accumulate as Pending. When it restarts, it lists unbound pods and drains the backlog — its only state is the ledger, so there is no journal to replay. A dead scheduler costs you placement latency, nothing else — compare an orchestrator that proxies work to its workers or holds placements in memory, where the master's crash is the cluster's outage.

Filter and score are plugin points in what Kubernetes calls the scheduling framework, alongside less famous phases (pre-filter, reserve, permit, pre-bind). One scheduler binary can run several profiles — distinct plugin configurations under different scheduler names — and a pod selects one with spec.schedulerName. And because binding is an ordinary authenticated write, a custom scheduler needs no hooks into the core: it is any program that watches for unbound pods and POSTs bindings. A toy one fits in a couple hundred lines.
sections.pattern: Separate deciding from acting: have the decider publish its choice as a durable record in the shared store, and let executors discover and act on it through their own subscriptions. The decision then survives the decider's crash, the decider stays out of the data path, and any process with write access can replace or supplement it.

sections.title: The reconciler at the edge
paras: Every loop so far has run inside the control plane. The kubelet — the node agent, one process per machine — is the same shape shipped to the edge. Its desired state is the set of pod specs bound to its node, watched from the API server with a field selector on spec.nodeName; its actual state is the set of containers running on the machine beneath it. The kubelet is a reconciler whose actuator is a container runtime instead of a REST API. Nothing pushes commands to it; scheduling was a field write, and the kubelet notices.

It does not run containers itself. It speaks the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), a gRPC API implemented by a runtime such as containerd or CRI-O: pull this image, create a pod sandbox (the shared network namespace the pod's containers live in), start these containers, report their states. The interface exists because the coupling it replaced was a failure mode — the kubelet once drove Docker through version-fragile glue code, and every runtime change rippled through the kubelet. Kubernetes runs no containers anywhere; it is management all the way down, delegating execution at the last step.

Probes feed the actual-state side. A startup probe holds the others off until a slow-booting process is up. A liveness probe failing means the process is wedged: the kubelet restarts the container, with exponential backoff between attempts so a crash-looping container cannot pin the node — you have seen this as CrashLoopBackOff. A readiness probe failing means something softer: the pod is removed from its Service's endpoints, the addresses traffic is balanced across, but the container is left running. The distinction matters because restarting an overloaded server destroys its warm state and amplifies the overload; taking it out of rotation lets it recover — restart the deadlocked, drain the busy.

There is a wake-up problem the control plane never had: containers die below Kubernetes — an OOM kill or a segfault happens in the kernel and the runtime, and no API event announces it. The PLEG — pod lifecycle event generator — closes the gap. Historically it relisted every container's state from the runtime roughly once a second, diffed against a cache, and turned each change into an event that wakes the per-pod sync workers. Newer kubelets can subscribe to evented streams from the CRI instead, keeping a slower relist as the backstop. It is the doctrine from the reconcile section again: watch for speed, rescan for truth.

Information flows the other way through the same door. The kubelet writes what it observes — container states, probe results, the pod's IP — into each pod's status subresource, and its node's conditions into the Node object. It writes observations, never desires, and it writes them to the API server, never to a controller. No controller calls a kubelet to ask; they watch the status it publishes. Spec flows down, status flows up, and the hub sees everything.

Node health is the same reporting discipline made cheap: each kubelet renews a Lease object — a record whose meaningful content is one renew timestamp — roughly every ten seconds. Heartbeats get a dedicated tiny object because the alternative was a failure mode: rewriting the large Node status every few seconds across a few thousand nodes is an etcd write storm, while a Lease renewal is a few hundred bytes. The node controller, a loop inside kube-controller-manager, watches these leases: silence for roughly forty seconds marks the node NotReady; silence for roughly five minutes triggers eviction, deleting the node's pods so their controllers reschedule them elsewhere. Two timescales, because the two mistakes carry different prices: flagging a node through a network blip is cheap, but mass-evicting healthy pods is a self-inflicted outage. This is the machinery behind the dead-node walkthrough — nothing detected a failure; a timestamp went stale.

One capability breaks the pattern on purpose. The kubelet also watches a directory of manifest files on local disk and runs any pod spec it finds there — static pods, no API server involved — then reports read-only mirror pods upward so they appear in kubectl. This resolves the bootstrap circularity: the API server runs as a pod, but pods normally come from the API server. On a control-plane node, kubeadm (the standard installer) writes etcd and kube-apiserver manifests to disk, the kubelet starts them from those files, and the cluster's first watch connection goes to an API server the kubelet itself brought up. The system hosts itself: the loop at the edge is the loop that boots the center.

sections.title: One driver at a time
paras: Run the control plane on one machine and that machine is your cluster's single point of failure. The fix differs per component, because each has a different relationship to state. API servers hold no authoritative state of their own — everything durable lives in etcd — so you run two or three of them active-active behind a load balancer, and any replica can serve any request. Statelessness is what makes horizontal replication free: there is no session to migrate and no local cache that must be authoritative.

etcd is the opposite case: it is the state, and Raft commits nothing without a majority — a quorum. So you run 3 or 5 members: 3 tolerates one failure, 5 tolerates two. Even counts buy nothing — 4 members still tolerate only one failure, because quorum rises to 3 while adding a fourth machine that can fail. Odd numbers only.

The scheduler and the kube-controller-manager — the process bundling the core reconciliation loops — are stateless too, but replicating them active-active would run the same loops twice against the same state. Two live controller-managers would each observe a ReplicaSet short one pod and each create one; two schedulers would race to bind every pending pod. Write-time guards would prevent corruption — a pod binds only once, and the CAS from section 04 rejects stale updates — but you would pay in constant conflicts and surplus pods. So these components run active-passive: several replicas, exactly one doing work. Which raises the question of who decides.

Kubernetes does not answer with a coordination service: leader election is a Lease, an ordinary API object in the coordination.k8s.io group whose interesting fields are holderIdentity, renewTime, and leaseDurationSeconds. To become leader you read the Lease, check that it is empty or expired, and write your own identity into it — against the resourceVersion you read, the same optimistic-concurrency check that guards every other write. If another candidate wrote first, your version is stale and you get 409 Conflict: you lost, resume polling. Election is not a new mechanism — it is one more compare-and-swap, serialized by the same Raft log as everything else. The failure mode avoided is a second consensus system to deploy, secure, upgrade, and page on alongside etcd.

In steady state the leader renews renewTime every couple of seconds; standbys re-read it on the same cadence and sit idle. Kill the leader and renewals stop; after roughly fifteen seconds the lease is expired in every standby's eyes, their next reads all attempt the acquiring write, and etcd serializes them — exactly one succeeds, the rest see 409. The brief leaderless window costs nothing, because the loops are level-triggered: the new leader lists current state and finds every piece of pending work already in it. Nothing sat queued in the dead leader's memory that a fresh list cannot reconstruct.

Be honest about what the Lease does not give you. A leader that pauses — a long GC pause, a frozen VM — rather than dies can wake after expiry still believing it leads, and act for a moment while its successor is already working. Lock-based systems need fencing tokens to survive this. Kubernetes absorbs it instead: updates built from the stale leader's pre-pause view carry old resourceVersions and land as 409, and any duplicate it manages to create is surplus for the next idempotent reconcile to delete. The Lease exists to prevent duplicate work; safety lives in the CAS on each individual write.

Now run the experiment end to end: kill -9 any control-plane component. An API server drops out of the load-balancer pool and clients retry against another replica. A scheduler or controller-manager loses its lease and a standby takes over, rebuilding its view through the same list-and-watch a normal start uses. etcd, down one member, keeps committing on quorum. Nothing is corrupted anywhere, because no component held state that only it knew — recovery is not a separate code path that runs rarely and rots; it is the reconcile loop, the code path that runs every second of every ordinary day.

This is the payoff of the choice from section 04. A lock-based design would have demanded a lock service, liveness detection, and fencing — three new mechanisms, each a fresh source of outages. Compare-and-swap demanded nothing new: election is a write, split-brain safety is a write, recovery is a re-read. One concurrency primitive, applied without exception, stretches from updating a pod's labels to deciding which process runs the cluster.

sections.title: What to Steal
paras: Store intent as versioned data in one place. Kubernetes components do not coordinate by calling each other; work is handed off through versioned records in one store, and the record is the interface. A record outlives crashes on both sides of a conversation, so a reader that was down for ten minutes wakes up to find the truth waiting — a dropped RPC or missed message has no such recovery. Steal this for deploy pipelines and provisioning systems: write the desired release as a versioned row, and make every worker act from the row, never from a call.

Declare desired state; never send imperative commands. "Three replicas" is safe to deliver twice, late, or out of order; "add one replica" is safe under none of those, because its meaning depends on state the sender only guessed at. In a billing reconciler, store the balance each account should be at instead of emitting charge events — duplicated or reordered events corrupt a ledger, a stated target cannot.

Level-triggered reconciliation, events as hints. Every controller compares desired state against observed state and fixes the difference; a notification only says "look now," it never carries the work itself. That is what makes a missed event survivable — the fatal flaw of edge-triggered designs, where one dropped message leaves the system permanently wrong. Sync engines want this shape: on every pass, diff the full current state against the target instead of trusting that you saw every change.

Idempotent, convergent actions. Every reconcile step is written to run twice safely: create-if-absent, delete-if-present, patch-toward-target. Retries and restarts then cost nothing, which is what lets recovery be the ordinary path instead of a feared one. Payment systems know this as idempotency keys; provisioning systems should say "ensure the VM exists," never "create the VM."

Optimistic concurrency over locks. A writer submits its change against the version it read, the store rejects stale writes with 409 Conflict, and the loser re-reads and retries — the pattern behind resourceVersion. A lock holder that dies stalls everyone behind it until a lease expires; a failed compare-and-swap costs one retry and blocks nobody. Any system where many writers touch shared rows — inventory, IaC state, seat assignment — should reach for CAS before it reaches for a mutex.

Watch plus local cache plus periodic resync. Controllers read from an in-memory cache fed by a change stream; when the stream breaks, the client re-lists from the store to heal the cache, and a periodic resync re-queues what is already cached so reconcile logic re-checks it. Naive polling melts the store as clients multiply; with a shared cache, thousands of read paths cost the store almost nothing, and resync bounds how long a skipped reconcile can last. This is the shape for config distribution and feature flags: push changes, cache locally, reconcile fully on a slow timer.

Many small loops, no orchestrator brain. A Deployment rollout is a chain of controllers, each managing the resource one level down — Deployment to ReplicaSet to Pod — coordinating only through the records they write. A central orchestrator accumulates the cross-product of every workflow's states and becomes unmodifiable; small loops fail, restart, and get replaced independently. Split your deploy pipeline into stages that each watch one table and write the next.

Crash-only, stateless workers. Outside the store itself, control-plane components keep no durable state; on restart they re-list, rebuild their caches, and resume mid-flight work — startup and recovery are the same code path. Graceful-shutdown logic is the least-tested code in most systems, and it is exactly the code that runs during your worst outage. Build workers you can kill -9 at any moment, and every deploy becomes a rehearsed recovery.

One uniform machinery for extensions. A CRD (CustomResourceDefinition) gives a user-defined type the same storage, versioning, watches, access control, and admission checks as built-in types — extensions enter through the front door, not a weaker side API. That is why the operator ecosystem grew: third-party controllers compose with everything else because they are indistinguishable from the core. If you build a platform, run your own features through the extension mechanism; the moment you keep a private, better API for yourself, the public one rots. And carry one sentence out of this whole deep dive: a Kubernetes cluster is a database of intent plus an army of janitors — an architecture that ports to nearly any system whose job is to keep reality matching a plan.

sections.title: The packet that never meets the Service
paras: The walkthrough gave every Service a stable address: the pods behind web.shop churn while 10.96.0.12 holds still. The natural mental model is that something answers at that address — a load-balancer process accepting connections and forwarding them. Go looking for it and there is nothing to find. No process anywhere listens on a ClusterIP. No pod holds the address; it exists only as a row in the ledger and as rewrite rules on every node.

The naive design — a real box in the middle — costs what middleboxes always cost: an extra hop on every connection, a throughput ceiling, one more failure that takes all traffic with it. Watch the packet instead: where its destination changes, and what never touches it.

The rewrite happens in the client node's kernel. kube-proxy runs on every node, but despite the name it proxies nothing: it is a controller that watches Services and EndpointSlices and compiles them into kernel rules — iptables chains or IPVS tables — that DNAT a packet's destination from the ClusterIP to a real pod IP as it leaves. eBPF dataplanes like Cilium can drop kube-proxy entirely and install the same logic as kernel programs. Either way, no process sits in the data path. The failure mode this kills is the middlebox: a hop that must scale with traffic and takes every flow down with it when it dies.

The set of legal rewrite targets is itself an object. The EndpointSlice controller watches pods and maintains, per Service, the list of backend IPs — each entry a target only while its pod passes its readiness probe, which is how the kubelet's probe verdicts reach routing: a pod failing readiness drops out of every node's rules without being restarted. When a backend dies, the update is pure ledger: the kubelet reports the pod gone, the EndpointSlice controller trims the list, and every node's kube-proxy sees the watch event and reprograms. No node tells another node anything; a thousand rule tables converge because all watch the same record.

Naming runs on the same machinery. CoreDNS resolves web.shop.svc to the ClusterIP — no privileged infrastructure, just a pod running a controller that watches Services and answers from cache. Ingress repeats this one layer up: an Ingress object is routing data in the ledger, and an ingress controller — an ordinary pod running nginx or envoy — watches those objects and rewrites its own configuration. Watch-and-reconcile does not care whether it programs a kernel table, a DNS zone, or a reverse proxy.

sections.title: Storage: a claim, not a disk
paras: Everything the control plane has managed so far is disposable. A pod dies, the ReplicaSet stamps out an identical replacement, and nothing is lost — because nothing was kept. A database breaks that assumption: its data must outlive any pod, any node, and ideally the app team's knowledge of which cloud it runs on.

Kubernetes answers with the split it uses everywhere: separate the request from the thing. The app team writes a PersistentVolumeClaim — "10Gi, class fast" — and never names a disk. In the figure, watch which cards are still lit after the pod is gone: that is the durable half of the system.

A PersistentVolumeClaim is desired state: a size and a storageClassName, written by the app team. A PersistentVolume is the record of an actual disk, cloud volume ID included. Binding matches them — the same intent/observation split as spec and status, stretched across two objects. The StorageClass names an external provisioner, and that CSI controller is another reconcile loop, running out-of-tree: watch for unbound claims, call the cloud API, post a PersistentVolume back to the ledger.

CSI is storage's CRI: a gRPC contract — CreateVolume, ControllerPublishVolume to attach a disk to a node, NodeStageVolume and NodePublishVolume to mount it — onto the node once, then into each pod. Before CSI, vendor drivers lived in the Kubernetes tree, so a cloud SDK bug shipped inside core and waited for the next Kubernetes release to fix; the contract lets vendors patch on their own schedule. One problem remains: a disk provisioned before scheduling can land in a zone the pod never reaches. volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer defers provisioning until the scheduler places the pod, so the disk is created where the pod runs — scheduler and storage negotiating through the ledger, never calling each other.

Delete the pod and the mount is released, but the claim, the volume, and the data stay — the claim is the durable object, and pods are temporary attachments to it. Deleting the claim is the real decision point: reclaimPolicy decides whether the underlying disk is destroyed (Delete) or kept — PersistentVolume and data intact — for manual recovery (Retain). StatefulSets close the loop for replicated databases: each pod gets a stable ordinal name — pg-0, pg-1 — and a claim template keyed to that name, so a replacement pg-1 re-finds pg-1's claim instead of an empty disk.

sections.title: Teach the ledger a new noun
paras: Every mechanism in this deep dive — the watch streams, the reconcile loops, the ownerReferences, the leases — has been serving Kubernetes' own types. So here is the question the whole architecture has been building toward: what does it take for the ledger to hold a noun Kubernetes has never heard of, like PostgresCluster?

In most platforms the answer is fork the core or bolt a second API alongside it, and the fork is where extensions go to rot. Watch for three things: a new type arriving as plain data, its endpoint live before anything restarts, and an ordinary pod running the same loop the built-ins run — handling a database failover with nobody paged.

A CustomResourceDefinition is itself an object you POST to the API server: the schema for a new type, expressed as data. Because the request pipeline contains no per-type logic — section 03's payoff — the server starts serving the type immediately: REST endpoints under /apis/db.acme.io/v1/postgresclusters, storage in etcd, RBAC verbs, watch streams, kubectl support, even the spec/status split once the CRD opts into the status subresource — with zero changes to Kubernetes code and no restart. The failure mode this kills is the fork: a core recompiled per type turns every extension into a patch you carry forever.

An operator is that CRD plus a controller you write, running the same informer, workqueue, and reconcile loop as the built-ins — controller-runtime and kubebuilder package client-go's machinery so you write little beyond the reconcile function. Your controller ships as an ordinary Deployment: a client like every other, entering through the same door, bound by the same RBAC. Seeing a PostgresCluster, it creates the StatefulSet, Services, and Secrets with ownerReferences pointing back, so deleting the parent lets garbage collection sweep the children. The point is to encode operational knowledge — provisioning, backup, upgrade, failover — as a loop over a domain object: when the primary dies, the reconciler promotes the replica, repoints the Service, and writes status, instead of a human working a runbook at 3am.

One honest caveat: an operator is software you now maintain, and a careless loop can fight the built-in controllers over the same children — so idempotency and level-triggered discipline matter more, not less. The meta-pattern is the capstone: the extension mechanism is the core mechanism. The Deployment controller uses no API your controller cannot; nothing the built-ins rely on is privileged, and that is the strongest evidence for the design — its authors chose to live inside it.
